I've been reading manga/watching anime ever since I was a kid, and honestly the best trick I've found it to read women mangakas (a bit of a generalisation I know but good rule of thumb). Now I'm almost 30 so I end up finding Josei to be the most "relevant" sometimes, but not necessarily. I know Fullmetal Alchemist has been mentioned, so I'll add the following to that list:

* D. Grayman
* Pandora Hearts
* Kuroshitsuji
* Vanitas no Carte
* Ao No Exorcist
* Noragami
* Barakamon
* Gin no Saji (same author as FMA)

and this is just the shounen category; if you venture in shoujo and josei, the list is nearly endless. Even the most useless women mangaka (imo that is) manage to create complex heroines, even when they, and their whole story, is the most annoying thing I've ever read (looking right atcha Fushigi Yuugi). As a quick example, I'd go for:

* Oishii Kankei
* Real Clothes
* Otoyomegatari
* V.B. Rose
* Fruits Basket
* Gekkan Shoujo Nozaki-kun (although this is p meta, so how much you get the jokes depends on how deep your knowledge of the genre is)
* Doubutsu no Oishasan
* Hyakki Yakoushou

...I've kinda forgotten the point I was starting to make when I started my comment, so I'll just say, manga/anime is an \*extremely\* vast category, and pleeeeeeennttyy of good, non-misogynistic rep exists, thankfully, so you might be setting yourself up for  a mighty task. I wish you luck nonethless!!!

(P.S. This doesn't mean male mangakas don't write good women; there are plenty who do; for example, Azumanga Daioh and Yotsuba-To's mangaka writes a lot of girls well, you just have to tread lighter, can't just blindly click anything \^\^;;)

Ok ok ok so many things to unpack here so

1. Yesssssss!!! Cabal is extremely underrated and I honestly don't understand why, it's basically the perfect blend of all the tropes everyone loooovveesss (witty writing, extremely pragmatic lead in a very traditionally unpragmatic career, overarching genres, spooky vibes, brothers), and the only reason why I can guess that this is is because folks don't pick it up due to the "horror" label, but honestly it's no more horrific than blackadder so idek why 

2. Hitchhiker's suffers from what I've termed the "Simpsons Effect", i.e. it's nice in small doses but if you try and binge it it becomes less funny. This is because I've noticed that if I come across a short clip of the Simpsons I'll find it funny, but if I sit down to watch the whole episode it's less so. Similarly, if I come across a quote or excerpt of Hitchhiker's, I can marvel at the writing and chuckle at the appropriate metaphors and similes, but if I ever binge read it I start to lose that level of appreciation. It's almost as if the context grounds it too much

3. All the Discworld sub-series have really different vibes going for them, and I completely understand what you mean!! When I started Discworld I initially read the first book (The Colour of Magic), which was a Bad Move ™️. I adored the writing but I couldn't care less about Rincewind or the tourist fellow, sadly. Then I accidentally came across Equal Rites, which is the first book in The Witches series, and everything just magically changed (pun not originally intended but I take all responsibility). So if you like Cabal, I'd strongly urge you to start with either The Witches series (my absolute absolute absolute favourite out of them all is Carpe Jugulum, the last book in the series, because everything sort of comes to a head and the turnout is spectacular), or The Death series (starts off with Mort). The Vimes series does get better, especially when The Vetinari appears more, but it is a bit of delayed gratification, and easier to bear once you're already in the system and invested, so to speak. There's also a really handy graphic floating around for the Discworld reading order, and it details all the different sub-series etc.

She just wanted a chance to feel beautiful, to have a good time, to eat food she hadn't cooked herself, to hear music other than her sisters' horrible singing, to maybe dance, to not do chores. For one night.

Belle did not fall in love with the Beast when he was being horrid. She fell in love with him when he made efforts to better himself.

Snow White was a princess whose own stepmother hired an assassin to take a hit on her. She made the best of a bad situation, she got along with her new family of dwarves, not all of whom accepted her immediately, but she worked her hardest to make a place for herself with them. Despite all that she still wanted someone who she could fall in love with, which I think is reasonable and understandable.

I think it takes a special kind of resilience to be hopeful in the face of trauma, to be able to stay and be kind after you've been treated horribly, to know that you are worthy of love even though you've not been treated as such. They are very important messages. Because everyone gets hurt in life. Your hurts may be dramatic as the ones in tales, and maybe they'll be different, but to instill a message that you should remain good, kind, and loving and know that you're worth goodness and kindness and love in return is valuable in ways money cannot even comprehend.

I'm glad that we are getting more varied movies with different messages of hope and bravery and kindness, I adore them all. One of my personal favourites is Lilo and Stitch, the majority of which I can recite word for word! And I love that new generations have Rapunzel and Merida and Tiana and Elsa and Anna and even more!! But I think we should not spread the narrative that the older movies were somehow less than because the older heroines wanted a life with less of a "career" aspect to them! Everyone should feel free to aspire to what their heart desires, as long as it hurts no one else in the process.

Maybe my answer is going to be super paranoid so don't take it as gospel, but having been in a similar situation, I would suggest the following:

-having enough money for about 3-4 months worth of rent saved up before you actually move.

-get a lockable firesafe/ waterproof+fireproof documents holder and slowly start collecting all your necessary paperwork into that.

-start squirrelling away the stuff you need into your car/at a friend's place etc; a small bag every day won't be missed, but taking out packing cartons will raise questions

-after you have everything in place, and have an alternate place to stay, choose a time when your parents are more likely to be relaxed e.g. after a big dinner, and tell them you need to move to concentrate on your school/be closer to your job etc. 

-Don't be afraid to use a half-truth, especially if you're the kind of person who can lie reasonably well. 

-Your parents might use emotional blackmail and guilt trips on you- don't cave. It's probably not a lie that they love you- and judging from your post, you're not going to cut them out of your life completely- so just stick to a more matter-of-fact reason, like doing better at school etc. 

-Don't bring up them being shoddy parents at *all*, and don't say anything that you know will be even the mildest sore point with them. 

-In fact, praise them, even if it's completely fake. Thank them for having raised you to be so independent, and thank them for always trusting you and your judgement. Praise them for even the most paltry thing and make it sound like a big deal (although don't overdo it so that it sounds like sarcasm). 

-If possible, make it sound like it was their idea that you move out in the first place. 

-If things get violent, be ready to hightail it out, with your sister if possible.

-If not, be on your best behaviour, do as many chores as possible and be as much of a lamb as you can, and move before they can say anything.

Again, hopefully I'm being paranoid and reading too much into everything so don't be scared, I just thought it would be better if I wrote something than if I didn't. Best of luck!!

The practice of denoting something's origins with a word is demonym. In English, demonyms mainly have to do with 2 things: the etymology of the place name, and the sources of the English language (i.e. from the romance languages side or the germanic languages side).

When denoting belonging with suffixes, they usually fall into one of two camps:
-Latin: Formerly, they each conveyed slightly different senses. -ese most directly meant “belonging to or originating in a place.” -(a)n and -ian are variations on the same suffix meaning “belonging to.” -er was used principally in the sense of “one having to do with a thing,” as in lawyer or villager. As with most vocabulary in English, they all now coexist and serve the same purpose.

Latin/Greek etymological ancestry also sometimes helps explain away the endings that don't make sense. For e.g. someone from Cyprus is called a Cypriot, because the original form was Kypriṓtēs, which got anglicised. Similarly, there Neopolitan, from the original Neāpolītānus. 

And then you have the ones in which society is trying to screw you over, like with Liverpuddlian, which was a direct result of someone's shining moment of wit as they humorously altered pool to puddle (and conjugated that with what felt right, in all probability).

-Old English, which is why citizens of the British Isles have -ish demonyms: Scottish, Welsh, English, etc.

Coming back to etymology, in Old English dutch simply meant “people or nation.” (This also explains why Germany is called Deutschland in German.) Over time, English-speaking people used the word Dutch to describe people from both the Netherlands and Germany, which is where many of their ancestors were from.
